latest_nl_proof:
Let
S_x = {km : k \in \mathbf Z_{\ge 0}} \cup \bigcup_{r=1}^{m-1} \{qm+r : q \in \mathbf Z_{\ge 0},\ q \ge x_r\}.
We will prove that S_x is a numerical semigroup and that its multiplicity is m.

Since m \ge 2 and each x_r is a positive integer, every element listed in the definition of S_x is a nonnegative integer. Also 0=0\cdot m belongs to S_x. Thus S_x \subseteq \mathbf Z_{\ge 0} and 0\in S_x.

It remains to prove:
(1) S_x is closed under addition;
(2) \mathbf Z_{\ge 0}\setminus S_x is finite;
(3) the least positive element of S_x is m.

First, closure under addition.
Take arbitrary a,b\in S_x. We consider cases according to how a and b are represented.

Case 1: both are multiples of m.
Write a=k_1m and b=k_2m with k_1,k_2\in \mathbf Z_{\ge 0}. Then
a+b=(k_1+k_2)m \in S_x.

Case 2: one is a multiple of m and the other is not.
Suppose a=k_1m with k_1\in \mathbf Z_{\ge 0}, and b=q_2m+r with r\in\{1,\dots,m-1\} and q_2\ge x_r. Then
a+b=(k_1+q_2)m+r.
Since k_1+q_2\ge q_2\ge x_r, we have a+b\in S_x. The same argument applies if the roles of a and b are reversed.

Case 3: neither is a multiple of m.
Then there exist i,j\in\{1,\dots,m-1\} and integers q_1,q_2\in \mathbf Z_{\ge 0} such that
a=q_1m+i, \qquad b=q_2m+j,
with q_1\ge x_i and q_2\ge x_j.
Now
a+b=(q_1+q_2)m+(i+j).
We split into three subcases.

Subcase 3a: i+j<m.
Then
a+b=(q_1+q_2)m+(i+j).
By hypothesis, x_i+x_j\ge x_{i+j}. Since q_1\ge x_i and q_2\ge x_j,
q_1+q_2 \ge x_i+x_j \ge x_{i+j}.
Hence a+b belongs to the part of S_x corresponding to residue i+j, so a+b\in S_x.

Subcase 3b: i+j=m.
Then
a+b=(q_1+q_2+1)m,
which is a nonnegative multiple of m. Therefore a+b\in S_x.

Subcase 3c: i+j>m.
Then i+j-m\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, and
a+b=(q_1+q_2+1)m+(i+j-m).
By hypothesis, x_i+x_j+1\ge x_{i+j-m}. Also q_1\ge x_i and q_2\ge x_j, so
q_1+q_2+1 \ge x_i+x_j+1 \ge x_{i+j-m}.
Hence a+b belongs to the part of S_x corresponding to residue i+j-m, so a+b\in S_x.

All cases give a+b\in S_x. Therefore S_x is closed under addition.

Second, co-finiteness.
Let
M=\max\{x_1,\dots,x_{m-1}\}.
This maximum exists because there are finitely many coordinates. We claim that every integer n\ge mM belongs to S_x.

Indeed, let n\ge mM. Divide n by m: there exist q\in \mathbf Z_{\ge 0} and r\in\{0,1,\dots,m-1\} such that
n=qm+r.
Since r\ge 0, we have q=(n-r)/m \ge (n-(m-1))/m, but in fact the simpler estimate suffices: from n=qm+r and r\le m-1 we get q\ge M when r=0 obviously if n=qm with q\ge M, and when r>0, n\ge mM implies qm+r\ge mM, hence q cannot be less than M unless q\le M-1, which would give qm+r\le (M-1)m+(m-1)=Mm-1<n, contradiction. So q\ge M.
Therefore, if r=0 then n=qm is a multiple of m and lies in S_x. If 1\le r\le m-1, then q\ge M\ge x_r, so n=qm+r\in S_x.
Thus every n\ge mM lies in S_x. Hence \mathbf Z_{\ge 0}\setminus S_x \subseteq \{0,1,\dots,mM-1\}, so the complement is finite.

Therefore S_x is a cofinite submonoid of \mathbf Z_{\ge 0}; that is, S_x is a numerical semigroup.

Third, the multiplicity.
Because m=1\cdot m\in S_x, S_x has a positive element, so its multiplicity is well-defined. We now show that m is its least positive element.

Certainly m\in S_x. On the other hand, no integer in \{1,2,\dots,m-1\} belongs to S_x: such a number is not a multiple of m, and if it equals qm+r with 1\le r\le m-1, then necessarily q=0. But 0\not\ge x_r because x_r>0. So it is not in the residue-r part of S_x.

Also, every non-multiple element of S_x has the form qm+r with q\ge x_r\ge 1 and 1\le r\le m-1, hence
qm+r \ge m+r > m.
So among positive elements of S_x, the smallest is the multiple m.

Therefore the multiplicity of S_x is m.

We have proved that S_x is a numerical semigroup and that its multiplicity equals m, exactly as claimed.
role_in_parent: Defines the backward map Psi from Kunz tuples to numerical semigroups and proves it lands among semigroups of multiplicity m.
statement_nl: Fix an integer m >= 2 and a tuple x=(x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers. Define S_x to be the set consisting of all nonnegative multiples of m and, for each r in {1,...,m-1}, all integers q m + r where q is a nonnegative integer and q >= x_r. If for every i,j in {1,...,m-1} one has: if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, then S_x is a numerical semigroup and its multiplicity is m.

domain_restrictions: S_x ⊆ Z_{>=0} (elements are nonnegative by construction: km and qm+r with k,q >= 0 and r>=1)
S_x contains all nonnegative multiples of m: {k m : k ∈ Z_{>=0}} (in particular 0 ∈ S_x)
For each r ∈ {1,...,m-1}, S_x contains exactly the numbers of the form q m + r with q ∈ Z_{>=0} and q >= x_r
Indexing constraints when inequalities are invoked: if i+j<m then i+j ∈ {1,...,m-1}; if i+j>m then i+j-m ∈ {1,...,m-1}
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: Let m be an integer with m>=2 and let x=(x_1,...,x_{m-1}) be positive integers. Define S_x = {k m : k ∈ Z_{>=0}} ∪ ⋃_{r=1}^{m-1} {q m + r : q ∈ Z_{>=0} and q >= x_r}. Assume that for all i,j ∈ {1,...,m-1}: (i+j<m ⇒ x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}) and (i+j>m ⇒ x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}). Then S_x is a numerical semigroup and its multiplicity equals m (i.e., the least positive element of S_x is m).

then (S_x is a numerical semigroup and multiplicity(S_x)=m)
